scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that knowledge reveals new mysteries, then argues it makes far more of the world understandable; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Every answer that science discovers seems to raise a host of new questions.
Some people argue that as we gain more knowledge, the world becomes not clearer but more complex and mysterious.
I agree that new knowledge often uncovers new mysteries, but I disagree that the world therefore becomes less understandable overall.

sections.role: Body 1 — Where the statement is true

sentences.text: First, it is true that learning more often reveals how much we still do not know.
Each discovery tends to open doors to deeper and harder questions.
For example, when physicists explained the atom, they uncovered a strange quantum world that puzzles experts to this day.
This shows that knowledge can expand the edge of mystery even as it grows.
Fields once thought simple, such as genetics, have turned out to be astonishingly complex.
The more we see, the more we realise how much remains hidden.
In this sense, the statement captures something real about inquiry.
Second, however, knowledge also makes a great deal of the world far more understandable.
Things that once seemed terrifying or magical now have clear and reassuring explanations.
Consider how diseases once blamed on curses are now understood as infections we can treat and prevent.
This kind of understanding has replaced fear with control across countless areas of life.
Knowledge also connects scattered facts into simple laws that explain many events at once.
A single idea like gravity can make sense of falling apples and orbiting planets together.
Overall, then, learning clarifies far more than it confuses.
In conclusion, gaining knowledge does reveal new mysteries at its frontier.
But at the same time it steadily turns confusion into understanding across the rest of life.
The world grows both clearer and more mysterious at once, and that double effect is the real nature of discovery.
